newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA TO TENDER FOR IMPORT OF 50,000T WHEAT.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA TO TENDER FOR IMPORT OF 50,000T WHEAT.

text.p: Bulgaria will call a tender by the end of the week for importing 50,000 tonnes of bread wheat to help cover its grain shortage until the new crop, Deputy Agriculture Minister Alexander Rangelov said on Wednesday.

He told Reuters the country now needed about 100,000 tonnes of wheat to cover the gap until the new crop, and a tender for importing 50,000 tonnes against the same quantity from the new crop was to be called within days.

"The agriculture ministry will set the terms of the deals which will be guaranteed by the government through the State Fund for Reconstruction and Development in a stable state-owned bank, probably the country's biggest, Bulbank," Rangelov said.
The tender for importing the other 50,000 tonnes of wheat is expected to be called by the end of the month, but the terms are yet to be decided upon, he added.
Bulgaria received 100,000 tonnes of wheat from Poland in March to ease its grain shortage against an agreement to export the same quantity of wheat from the new crop.
The country also awarded contracts to Swiss firm Glencore and Bulgaria's Nada to import 100,000 tonnes of wheat against forward contracts to export 134,000 tonnes from the new crop.
Another 35,000 tonnes of the new crop were approved to be bartered for combine harvesters and other equipment needed to improve the capacity of Bulgaria's outdated machinery.

Rangelov said the new crop, which he expected to be much better than last year's, will enable the country to meet its domestic consumption and to return the wheat which has been bought in exchange for future exports from the new crop.

Earlier this week, the ministry forecast 1997 wheat production at some 3.0 million tonnes, up from last year's 1.8 million tonnes. Bulgaria's domestic consumption is estimated at some 1.6 million tonnes.
"The expected wheat output and the imported quantities will be enough to meet domestic needs, service export commitments under forward contracts and put aside reserves," Rangelov said.
Excessive wheat exports two years ago and a bad harvest last year created acute grain shortages earlier this year, which have been overcome in the past three months.
Bulgaria sowed 1.5 million hectares with wheat and barley last year, up from 1.27 million hectares in the previous year.
